To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) HIV-infected adults with impaired ART response have fewer B cell subsets that produce antibodies against pneumococcal vaccine, and that 2) these B cell subset disturbances correlate with poor vaccine responsiveness.

the B cell subsets of HIV patients on ART are more similar to B cell subsets of uninfected individuals, while the B cell subsets among untreated HIV patients are more similar to those of HIV patients on antiretrovials with poor immune recovery.
B-cell perturbations are associated with poor response to pneumococcus vaccination in HIV patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of B-cell perturbations on vaccine response among HIV patients.
the development of novel vaccines for infectious diseases.
how HIV affects the human B cell compartment, and how this affects immune responses to vaccine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
B-cell perturbations are associated with poor response to pneumococcus vaccine in HIV-infected patients, especially in ART-responders.
B cell subset disturbances are associated to poor vaccine response among treated and untreated HIV infected patients.
HIV infection is associated with a profound perturbation of the B-cell repertoire and that these perturbations are associated with poor pneumocococcal conjugated vaccine responsiveness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV patients with a high proportion of isotype-switching memory B cells have a good response to pneumococal conjugate vaccine.
HIV-infected adults with low CD4+ cell counts have a higher risk of poor pneumococcocal conjugate vaccine response.
the immune response to pneumococcocal vaccine in HIV-infected adults is associated with B-cell subset disturbances, which can be improved by antiretrovial therapy.

B-cell subset perturbations are associated with poor pneumococca vaccine response.
